stem: Theories of aging are grouped into which four broad categories?
options: Stochastic, genetic, psychological, and sociological theories
Only biological and chemical theories
Only economic and political theories
Only nutritional and environmental theories

stem: Stochastic theories of aging are BEST described as being based on which assumption?
options: The cumulative effects of environmental assaults eventually become incompatible with life
Aging is entirely programmed by a single gene with no environmental influence
Aging results exclusively from social role changes
Aging is caused only by psychological adjustment to retirement

stem: The somatic mutation theory, a stochastic theory of aging, holds that aging results MOST from which of the following?
options: Prolonged exposure to background radiation causing cell mutations that eventually lead to death
A genetically programmed decline in hormone secretion
A decline in self-actualization needs
A loss of social roles following retirement

stem: The error theory, a stochastic theory of aging, is based on the belief that aging results MOST from which of the following?
options: Environmental changes that interfere with cell function and reproduction, causing errors that multiply in a geometric progression until cells are no longer viable
A single programmed genetic switch that activates at a fixed age
Social disengagement from society
A decline in satisfaction of interpersonal relationships

stem: The free radical theory of aging is based on the belief that aging is caused MOST by which of the following?
options: Damage caused by the action of free radicals, which are highly chemically reactive by-products of metabolism
A fixed genetic clock located exclusively in the hypothalamus
A decline in social roles and responsibilities
A conscious choice to withdraw from society

stem: According to the free radical theory, free radicals are normally destroyed by which of the following?
options: Protective enzyme systems within the body
External antibiotic therapy alone
Deliberate caloric restriction only
Increased exposure to background radiation

stem: Genetic theories of aging are based MOST on the assumption that aging is which of the following?
options: A part of the developmental process with differences in that process genetically programmed from conception
Caused entirely by cumulative environmental assaults with no genetic component
Caused entirely by social role loss
A product of psychological adjustment with no biological basis

stem: The neuroendocrine theory, a genetic theory of aging, holds that aging is the result of which of the following?
options: Functional decrements in neurons and their associated hormones
Random environmental radiation exposure
Social withdrawal from previously held roles
A decline in self-actualization needs

stem: The intrinsic mutagenesis theory, a genetic theory of aging, holds that each person has a genetic constitution that regulates which of the following?
options: The replication of genetic materials, which over time creates mutations that result in the effects of aging
Only the color of a person's hair with no other effect
Only the rate of a person's social disengagement
Only psychological adjustment to retirement

stem: The immunological theory, a genetic theory of aging, holds that aging is a function of which of the following?
options: Changes in the body's immune system as people age, as the body's immunological mechanisms perceive their own cells as foreign and destroy them
A purely psychological process of self-actualization
A decline in interpersonal trust during adolescence
A single fixed hormonal switch with no immune component

stem: Among psychological theories of aging, the Jungian psychoanalytic theory regards aging MOST as which of the following?
options: A time of developing self-awareness through reflective activity
A time of complete social withdrawal with no reflective component
A time defined exclusively by hormonal decline
A time of increasing interpersonal insecurity with no self-awareness

stem: Harry-Stack Sullivan's interpersonal theory, a psychological theory of aging, is developmental in nature and involves which of the following?
options: The development of satisfactory interpersonal relationships over time
The exclusive study of hormonal secretion patterns
A theory concerned only with genetic mutation rates
A theory concerned only with free radical accumulation

stem: According to Harry-Stack Sullivan's interpersonal theory, the loss of these relationships over time is believed to result in which of the following?
options: A loss of interpersonal security and the consequent psychological aspect of aging
An automatic increase in self-actualization
A decrease in chronic disease prevalence
An immediate reversal of biological aging

stem: Abraham Maslow's human needs theory, as applied to psychological aging, suggests that the greatest difficulty in meeting basic needs correlates MOST with which of the following?
options: The greater impact on the individual as they age
A complete absence of impact regardless of age
An impact limited strictly to adolescence
An impact limited strictly to early adulthood

stem: Erik Erickson's theory of psychosocial development, applied to the aging adult, suggests that the degree of success experienced in accomplishing developmental tasks across which stages influences the accomplishment of the task of the older adult?
options: Stages 1 through 7
Only stage 1
Only stage 8
Stages 9 through 12

stem: Sociological theories of aging focus MOST on which of the following?
options: The relationship at which individuals participate in their later years and adaptation to accepted social values
Exclusively the biochemical mechanisms of cellular aging
Exclusively the genetic mutation rate within cells
Exclusively the accumulation of free radicals in tissue

stem: The disengagement theory, a sociological theory of aging, proposes that aging is a developmental task that involves which of the following?
options: A process of withdrawal from society that permits the individual to enjoy old age and prepare for death without causing social disruption
Continued engagement with society at the same level as before
A process of continually acquiring new social roles
A rejection of all previously held personality traits

stem: The continuity theory, a sociological theory of aging, posits that an individual's behavior over time MOST reflects which of the following?
options: Continued engagement with society and the assumption of new roles and functions despite inability to engage with societal roles and functions
An abrupt and complete withdrawal from all social engagement
A total loss of personality traits acquired earlier in life
A fixed, unchanging behavior pattern from birth that requires no adaptation

stem: Which theory of aging holds that individuals change very little over time and that active, outgoing people when younger will behave in exactly the same way as they age?
options: Continuity theory
Disengagement theory
Activity theory
Age stratification theory

stem: The activity theory of aging holds that an older person, aware of certain failing skills, must make all the more effort to do which of the following?
options: Counter this deterioration by remaining active on others to maintain a sense of purpose and satisfaction
Withdraw completely from all social roles
Accept decline passively with no compensatory effort
Disengage from society to avoid social disruption

stem: According to activity theory, what is said to be a sign of 'healthy ageing'?
options: Remaining active in a manner that is the opposite of the disengagement theory
Complete withdrawal from society
A fixed, unchanging personality with no compensatory activity
Total loss of personal roles with no replacement activity

stem: The age stratification theory of aging focuses MOST on which of the following?
options: The interdependence between older adults and society, and how aging is viewed by others
Exclusively the biochemical mechanisms of free radical accumulation
Exclusively genetic mutation rates in somatic cells
Exclusively hormone secretion from the pituitary gland

stem: According to age stratification theory, it is society that determines which of the following?
options: Whether one is considered elderly or not, based on productivity used to define a person's age
The exact biochemical rate of free radical accumulation
The precise genetic mutation rate within an individual's cells
The exact hormonal decline curve of the neuroendocrine system

stem: Which myth/misconception about older adults is dispelled by the fact that aging affects each individual differently, with some playing golf and driving at age 85 while others do not?
options: Chronologic age determines oldness and aging is a uniform process
Old age is a time of tranquility and decreased resources
Older adults cannot live independently
Older adults are resistant to change

stem: Which myth/misconception about older adults is dispelled by evidence that most elderly retain mental faculties well beyond the ninth decade of life, with cognitive deficits typically caused by specific physical health risk factors rather than age alone?
options: Most elderly persons have diminished intellectual capacity or are senile
Older adults cannot live independently
Old age is a time of tranquility
Chronologic age determines oldness

stem: Senility, a term widely used to denote deteriorating mental faculties associated with old age, is affected by what percentage of people aged 65 years?
options: Less than 1%

stem: Which of the following is cited as a treatable cause of cognitive impairment or dementia-like symptoms in older adults, according to the notes?
options: Drug toxicity, metabolic disorders, depression, or hyperthyroidism
An irreversible fixed genetic mutation with no treatable component
A permanent and untreatable decline in crystallized intelligence
An untreatable decline in vocabulary and judgement

stem: According to research cited in the notes, which type of intelligence or ability is reported to actually IMPROVE with age?
options: Wisdom, judgement, vocabulary, creativity, common sense, coordination of facts and ideas, and breadth of knowledge and experiences
Reaction time speed
Short-term memory for novel information only
Visual acuity for fine print

stem: Which myth/misconception about older adults is dispelled by evidence that healthy older people usually remain productive, active, and involved rather than disengaging or isolating themselves?
options: Older adults cannot be productive or active
Old age is defined purely by chronologic age
Senility affects 100% of people above age 65
Older adults are universally resistant to change

stem: Which myth/misconception about older adults is addressed by the observation that many are forced to retire at a specific age despite continued productivity, and continue contributing through volunteer or artistic endeavors?
options: Older adults cannot be productive or active
Chronologic age determines oldness uniformly for all individuals
Senility is an inevitable and universal consequence of aging
Most older adults are resistant to change

stem: Which myth/misconception about older adults is dispelled by the observation that resistance to change tends to be a lifelong, relative personality characteristic rather than a trait acquired specifically in old age?
options: All older adults are resistant to change
Chronologic age determines oldness
Senility affects most elderly people
Older adults cannot live independently

stem: According to the notes, approximately what percentage of older adults live independently in the community, outside formal facilities?
According to the notes, approximately what percentage of older adults live in institutions such as nursing homes or extended care facilities?
Which physical characteristic of old age is described as marked by 'thinning and shrinkage,' resulting in a loss of height of about two inches by age 80?
options: Bone and joint changes
Digestive system changes
Eyesight changes
Voice changes

stem: Which chronic condition related to bone and joint changes is commonly associated with a stooping posture and greater susceptibility to home and joint diseases in older adults?
options: Osteoarthritis and osteoporosis
Presbyopia and cataracts
Chronic mucus hypersecretion
Dysphagia and constipation

stem: Chronic mucus hypersecretion (CMH) in older adults is defined MOST as which of the following?
options: Coughing and bringing up sputum, a common respiratory symptom in elderly persons
A disorder exclusively of the digestive system
A disorder exclusively of the reproductive system
A disorder exclusively affecting the eyes

stem: Dental problems in older adults MOST increase the chance of which of the following?
options: Tooth decay and infection due to less saliva and reduced ability for oral hygiene
Improved digestion with no complications
Enhanced sense of taste with no complications
Reduced risk of falls

stem: Which digestive system change is commonly noted in old age, marked by difficulty in swallowing and inability to eat enough?
options: Difficulty in swallowing, inability to eat enough, constipation, and bloating
Improved absorption of all nutrients with age
Enhanced salivation with age
A complete absence of any digestive change

stem: Presbyopia, an eyesight change common in old age, is marked MOST by which of the following?
options: Difficulty in reading especially small print in low lighting and difficulty locating objects also impaired by age 80
Improved near vision with age
Enhanced night vision with age
A complete absence of visual change with age

stem: Older adults are at increased risk of injury from falls MOST because of which of the following?
options: Falls that might not cause injury to a younger person can cause injury to older people and are a leading cause of injury and death
Falls affect only younger populations and spare the elderly entirely
Falls in old age never result in fracture or death
Falls are unrelated to bone and joint changes in old age

stem: Voice changes in old age are marked MOST by which of the following?
options: Vocal cords weakening and vibrating more slowly, resulting in a breathy voice sometimes called 'old person's voice'
An increase in vocal pitch with no change in breathiness
Complete loss of the ability to vocalize at any age over 65
An unrelated change confined only to younger populations

stem: According to Cox, Abramson, Devine, and Hollon (2012), which factor is cited as a risk factor for depression among older people when internalized?
options: Prejudice from others, known as 'anti-elderly prejudice,' turning inward and causing depression
A lack of any social contact whatsoever
Exclusively genetic mutation of neurons
Exclusively free radical accumulation in the brain

stem: Old age depression is associated with which notable statistic regarding suicide, according to the notes?
options: The over-65 population has the highest suicide rate among age groups
The over-65 population has the lowest suicide rate among all age groups
Suicide rates are identical across all age groups with no variation
Suicide risk decreases to zero after retirement

stem: The 'slowness behavior' described in old age refers MOST to which of the following?
options: A correlation between advancing age and slowness of reaction and physical and mental task performance
An increase in reaction speed with advancing age
A phenomenon unrelated to physical or mental task performance
A decrease in age correlating with increased slowness

stem: Psychological ageing refers MOST to which of the following?
options: Behavior changes, alteration in self-perception, and reactions to the biological changes of the body over time, giving rise to the concept of 'youth at heart'
Exclusively the biochemical process of cellular senescence
Exclusively the social roles assigned to an individual by society
Exclusively the chronological number of years a person has lived

stem: Sociological ageing refers MOST to which of the following?
options: The roles and social habits of the individual in society, closely related to functional ageing
Exclusively the biochemical process of free radical accumulation
Exclusively the number of chromosomes within a cell
Exclusively the pattern of hormone secretion from the pituitary gland

stem: Senescence, as defined in the notes, is BEST described as which of the following?
options: A process of aging and a multidimensional process of physical, psychological, and social change
A fixed event that occurs only at a specific birthday
A process confined strictly to the reproductive system
A term synonymous exclusively with chronological age

stem: Biological ageing refers MOST to which of the following?
options: Changes to structures and functions of the body that occur over the life span due to biological activities of the cells, tissues, and organs
Exclusively the social roles assigned to an individual
Exclusively the number of years since birth with no biological component
Exclusively the psychological reaction to retirement

stem: Functional ageing refers MOST to which of the following?
options: The capacities of an individual to function in society compared with others of the same age
Exclusively the number of chromosomes within a cell
Exclusively the accumulation of free radicals in tissue
Exclusively the genetic mutation rate of somatic cells

stem: In developed nations, the chronological age most commonly cited as roughly equivalent to retirement age and the beginning of old age is which of the following?
options: 60 or 65 years
25 years
35 years
45 years

stem: Chronological ageing is BEST described as which of the following?
options: How old a person is, referring to the actual amount of time a person has been alive, regardless of how healthy a lifestyle they lead
A measure exclusively of psychological adjustment
A measure exclusively of social role change
A measure exclusively of free radical accumulation

stem: Universal ageing, a distinction in ageing, refers MOST to which of the following?
options: Age change that all people share
Age change experienced only by a subset of the population, such as those with a specific disease
A localized age-based effect that comes from the recent past
An age-based difference traced back to a cause early in a person's life

stem: Probabilistic ageing, a distinction in ageing, refers MOST to which of the following?
options: Age changes that may happen to some, but not all people as they grow older, such as the onset of type two diabetes
Age change that all people share with no exception
The actual amount of time a person has been alive with no variability
An age-based difference traced back to childhood poliomyelitis

stem: Proximal ageing, a distinction in ageing, refers MOST to which of the following?
options: Age-based effects that come from a recent cause
Age-based effects that come from a cause early in a person's life, such as childhood poliomyelitis
Age change shared universally by all people
The actual chronological number of years since birth

stem: Distal ageing, a distinction in ageing, refers MOST to which of the following?
options: Age-based difference that can be traced back to a cause early in a person's life, such as childhood poliomyelitis
Age-based effects that come from a recent cause only
Age change shared universally with no individual variation
A measure exclusively of chronological years since birth

stem: Which of the following is listed as a genetic factor affecting the process of ageing?
options: Gene variations affecting telomere length, with shorter telomeres associated with earlier cellular senescence
Only the climate of the region a person lives in
Only the type of job a person holds
Only the frequency of medical check-ups

stem: Telomeres, cited in the notes as biological timers related to the genetic factor of ageing, are located MOST where within the cell?
options: In the nucleus of each cell, at the fourth pair of the twenty-three pairs of human chromosomes
Exclusively within the mitochondria with no nuclear component
Exclusively within the cell membrane
Exclusively within the Golgi apparatus

stem: According to the notes, people with shorter telomeres are at risk of which of the following?
options: Early ageing, because their telomeres diminish more quickly or because they were born with a shorter version of these genes
Delayed ageing with no increased cellular senescence risk
No change whatsoever in cellular senescence
An automatic increase in lifespan regardless of telomere length

stem: Which of the following is listed as a non-genetic factor affecting the process of ageing?
options: Family background, life style, nature of job, and environment
Exclusively the length of telomeres within chromosomes
Exclusively the presence of gene variations
Exclusively biological timers within the nucleus

stem: According to the notes, a nonstop pregnancy-lactation cycle, cited under fertility process as a factor affecting ageing, is believed to do which of the following?
options: Deprive the woman of nutritional reserve necessary for healthy living
Enhance nutritional reserve with no depletion whatsoever
Have no bearing whatsoever on a woman's ageing process
Exclusively affect bone density with no effect on nutritional reserve

stem: According to the notes, early termination of menstruation through removal of the ovaries via total abdominal hysterectomy leads MOST to which of the following?
options: Premature menopause and therefore hastens the ageing process due to lack of or insufficient hormones to support oestrogen
Delayed menopause with no hormonal consequence
An automatic increase in oestrogen production
No change whatsoever in the ageing process

stem: Poor personal and environmental hygiene, cited as a factor affecting the ageing process, includes which of the following examples?
options: Irregular bathing, improper care of the teeth, drinking unclean water, and leaving a dirty home environment
Regular bathing with clean water only
Routine dental cleaning with no adverse effect
A spotless home environment with no adverse effect

stem: Lack of exercise, cited as a factor affecting the ageing process, is believed to affect ageing MOST by which of the following mechanisms?
options: Regular exercise keeps the body active, aids nerve excitation, and keeps joints free from stiffness
Exercise has no bearing whatsoever on joint stiffness
Exercise exclusively affects dental health with no joint benefit
Exercise accelerates joint stiffness regardless of frequency

stem: Which of the following is listed among the ways to gracefully age, according to the notes?
options: Adoption of healthy lifestyles, good habit formation, regular exercise, and a balanced diet
Complete avoidance of all physical activity
Irregular medical check-ups with no adverse consequence
Poor habit formation with no adverse consequence

stem: Which of the following statements BEST reflects how socially constructed meanings of old age vary across developing nations, according to the notes?
options: In many parts of the developing world, chronological time plays little or no importance in the meaning of old age, with roles and physical decline playing a more significant part
Chronological age plays an identical role in defining old age in every developing nation with no variation
Old age is defined purely by retirement age in every society without exception
Old age has no social construction whatsoever in any society

stem: CASE SCENARIO: An 82-year-old client who was a reserved, solitary person throughout adulthood continues to prefer quiet solitary activities in the nursing home and shows no interest in group events, which she also avoided decades earlier. Which theory of aging BEST explains this client's stable pattern of behavior over time?
options: Continuity theory
Disengagement theory
Activity theory
Age stratification theory

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A 78-year-old retired teacher, aware that his short-term memory is not as sharp as before, deliberately joins a community book club, volunteers twice weekly, and maintains an active social calendar to compensate and remain fulfilled. Which theory of aging is MOST clearly being demonstrated?
options: Activity theory
Disengagement theory
Age stratification theory
Somatic mutation theory

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A 70-year-old woman had a total abdominal hysterectomy with removal of both ovaries at age 40 due to a gynecological condition, and her family notes that she appears to have developed osteoporosis and other signs of aging earlier than her peers. Which factor affecting the ageing process BEST explains this client's accelerated changes?
options: Early termination of menstruation leading to premature menopause and insufficient oestrogen
A purely genetic telomere-length effect unrelated to her surgical history
An unrelated effect of chronic mucus hypersecretion
An unrelated effect of chronic joint disease

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A community health nurse is asked to explain why two 70-year-old clients from the same neighborhood appear markedly different in physical ability, noting that one still plays golf and drives independently while the other requires full assistance with activities of daily living. Which concept BEST explains this difference despite identical chronological age?
options: Functional ageing varies between individuals of the same chronological age due to differing genetic, lifestyle, and health factors
Chronological ageing guarantees identical functional capacity for people of the same age
Universal ageing ensures all people experience decline at exactly the same rate
Distal ageing has no bearing on functional capacity in older adults

stem: CASE SCENARIO: An elderly client tells the nurse, 'Everyone treats me like I'm invisible and incompetent just because of my age, and lately I've started believing it myself and feeling hopeless.' Which concept from the notes BEST explains the psychological risk illustrated in this statement?
options: Internalized anti-elderly prejudice as a risk factor for depression in older adults
The somatic mutation theory of aging
The age stratification theory's purely sociological mechanism with no psychological component
The free radical theory of aging
